title: Type Inference
summary: How a compiler deduces types without explicit annotations — the mechanics behind var/auto/let and Hindley-Milner-style whole-program inference, and where it quietly breaks down.

slides.markdown:
Static typing (an earlier Topic) requires every value's type to be known before the program runs — but "known to the checker" doesn't have to mean "written out by hand." **Type inference** is the compiler deducing a value's type from context, so you get full static safety without annotating every single variable.

`let x = 5;` never states that `x` is a number, but the compiler knows it anyway — it looked at the right-hand side. That's local inference, and most modern statically typed languages (Java's `var`, C++'s `auto`, Kotlin's `val`) have some version of it. Some languages go much further: Haskell and OCaml can infer the type of an *entire function* purely from how it's used internally, with zero annotations anywhere, using an algorithm called Hindley-Milner.

This Topic is entirely a static-typing feature — a dynamically typed language has nothing to infer, since it never checks types ahead of time in the first place.

Without inference, static typing has a real cost: every variable needs an explicit type written out, even when the type is completely obvious from context. `Map<String, List<Integer>> scores = new HashMap<String, List<Integer>>();` repeats the same type twice for no informational gain — the right-hand side already determines what the left-hand side must be.

Inference removes that redundancy while keeping every one of static typing's guarantees intact: the compiler still verifies every operation is type-correct before the program runs; it just fills in the type annotation itself instead of requiring you to write it. `var scores = new HashMap<String, List<Integer>>();` in Java is exactly as type-checked as the fully annotated version — the compiler infers `scores`'s type from the constructor call, then proceeds to check everything downstream against that inferred type exactly as it would against an explicit one.

So inference is purely a **notation** improvement, not a safety trade-off — it's static typing with less to type, not a looser version of static typing.

slides.subTitle: var/auto/let inferring from the right-hand side
slides.markdown:
**Local inference** deduces a variable's type from its own initializer, looking only at that one line — it never has to consider how the variable is used afterward. `var count = 5;` in Java infers `int` purely from the literal `5`; `auto x = someFunction();` in C++ infers `x`'s type from `someFunction`'s declared return type; Kotlin's `val name = "Ada"` infers `String`.

The defining limitation, by design: local inference only looks *rightward and locally* — at the initializer expression — never at how the variable gets used later in the function. `var x = 5; x = "hello";` is a compile error in Java (`x` was inferred as `int`, and `String` can't be assigned to it), which is the same error you'd get with an explicit `int x = 5;` — inference didn't change the type-checking outcome at all, only who wrote the annotation down.

This is why local inference is considered "safe" enough to be uncontroversial in mainstream languages — it's a strict readability improvement with zero change in what programs are accepted or rejected.

Global inference (Hindley-Milner) works differently from local inference — instead of reading one line, it treats every unannotated type as a placeholder variable, then solves for all of them at once by walking the whole expression and collecting constraints.

For `let double = fun x -> x + x`, the algorithm doesn't look at `x`'s "declaration" (there isn't an explicit one) — it introduces a placeholder type for `x`, notices `x` is used with `+`, which constrains `x`'s type to whatever `+` requires (a number), propagates that constraint back to `x`'s placeholder, and concludes `double : int -> int` (or the generic numeric type, depending on the language) without a single type annotation anywhere in the source.

This constraint-solving process — called **unification**, the same underlying idea as Prolog's unification, applied here to type variables instead of logical terms — is why Hindley-Milner can infer whole function signatures: it doesn't need a starting annotation to anchor from, it derives every placeholder's concrete type from how all of them interact.

slides.subTitle: Hindley-Milner inferring whole-function signatures
slides.markdown:
Hindley-Milner (the algorithm behind ML, Haskell, and OCaml's inference) goes past "infer this one variable's type from its initializer" to "infer an entire function's type signature from its body, with zero annotations required anywhere, including the parameters."

`let compose f g x = f (g x)` gets a full, correctly generalized type — `compose : (b -> c) -> (a -> b) -> a -> c` — purely from how `f`, `g`, and `x` are combined inside the body. Nobody wrote `f`'s type; the algorithm derived that `f` must be a function whose argument type matches whatever `g x` produces, and that `g` must be a function whose argument type matches `x`'s (unconstrained, hence generic) type.

The payoff over local inference: you get full static type safety on genuinely generic, reusable functions without writing a single type annotation, and the inferred type is often the *most general* type possible for that function — meaning it doesn't over-constrain what argument types can be used with it, which is a stronger guarantee than "I annotated the type I happened to think of."

```haskell
-- No type annotation anywhere in this definition
identity x = x

-- GHCi (the Haskell REPL) reports its inferred type:
-- identity :: a -> a

-- Used with different types, still fully type-checked:
identity 5        -- a is inferred as Int for this call site
identity "hello"  -- a is inferred as String for this call site
identity True     -- a is inferred as Bool for this call site
```

`identity`'s body gives the algorithm exactly one constraint: the return value equals the parameter. There's nothing forcing `a` to be any specific type, so Hindley-Milner correctly generalizes it to a **type variable** `a` that can stand for any type — the function is generic not because the programmer wrote `<T>` anywhere, but because the algorithm found no constraint that would narrow it further.

This is the concrete version of "the algorithm derives the most general type possible" — a hand-written annotation might have accidentally been narrower (`identity :: Int -> Int`, if the author only had integers in mind), while inference finds the type that's actually justified by the code.

Inference isn't unconditional. Two concrete situations force you back to explicit annotations.

**Ambiguous call sites.** `var result = someOverloadedFunction();` — if the compiler can't determine which overload was intended purely from the call, or if the return type genuinely depends on information not present at that call site, inference has nothing to anchor on and either fails to compile or (worse) infers something you didn't intend.

**Public API boundaries.** A function's parameter and return types are part of its contract with every caller — inferring them from the function's *current* implementation means the signature can silently change if the implementation changes, which is exactly backwards from what a stable public API needs. This is why even languages with powerful inference (Kotlin, Rust) still require or strongly encourage explicit types on public function signatures: inference is for internal, throwaway, or genuinely-obvious-from-context values, not for the contract other code depends on.

The practical rule: infer locals and internal expressions freely; annotate anything that's a promise to a caller.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: over-relying on inference hurts public signatures
slides.markdown:
Even in languages that technically allow inferring a public function's return type from its body, doing so is a readability trap that compounds over time. `fun computeDiscount(order) = ...` with an inferred return type means a reader has to trace the entire function body — possibly several branches deep — just to answer "what does calling this give me back," a question an explicit `: Double` would answer in zero seconds.

Worse, the inferred type can silently change as the implementation evolves: today the function always returns a `Double`; a refactor adds a branch that returns `null` in an edge case, and the inferred return type widens to `Double?` without any explicit signal in the diff that the function's contract just changed for every caller. An explicit annotation would have forced that refactor to either update the annotation (making the contract change visible in the diff) or fix the branch to still satisfy the original type.

The rule this reinforces from the previous Subtopic: inference is a readability and ergonomics win for code whose type is genuinely obvious and internal; it's a liability at any boundary where the type *is* the documentation.

| | Local inference (Java `var`) | Full inference (Haskell) |
|---|---|---|
| **What it looks at** | Only the initializer expression on the same line | The entire function body, solving all placeholder types simultaneously |
| **Can infer a function's parameter types?** | No — parameters must be explicitly typed | Yes — including fully generic parameter types with no annotation |
| **Failure mode when ambiguous** | Compile error, usually easy to diagnose (look at the one line) | Can produce a confusing type error far from the actual mistake, since the constraint solver reports where propagation failed, not necessarily where the real error is |
| **Typical use** | Reducing redundant annotations on locals | Enabling fully generic, reusable functions with zero annotation ceremony |

The trade named in that third row is real and often surprising to newcomers: Hindley-Milner's error messages can point at a symptom several lines away from the actual mistake, because the solver only discovers a contradiction once enough constraints have accumulated — a cost of the algorithm's power that local inference, by only ever looking at one line, never incurs.

slides.sectionTitle: Why did the compiler infer this — and why did it fail here?
slides.markdown:
This exact framing — "why did the compiler infer this type, and why did it fail here" — tests whether you can trace inference's reasoning rather than treat it as a black box.

A good answer names the specific evidence the compiler used: "it inferred `x: Int` because the initializer `5` is an integer literal, and Kotlin's local inference reads only that right-hand side." And when inference *fails* — say, `var result = maybeGetValue();` where `maybeGetValue` is overloaded and the compiler can't determine which overload's return type to use — the strong answer identifies the missing piece of evidence specifically: "there's no argument-based way to disambiguate the overload at this call site, so the compiler has no single return type to infer `result` as, and needs either an explicit annotation on `result` or a more specific call."

The weak answer just says "the compiler couldn't figure out the type" without saying *what information was missing* — which reads as having memorized that inference sometimes fails, not understanding the mechanism well enough to predict when.

Inference is purely about *who writes the type annotation* — you or the compiler — and never about weakening what gets checked; every inferred program is exactly as type-safe as the fully annotated version of the same code. That's worth holding onto going into the rest of this group, where the Topics ahead (generics, variance, structural typing, ADTs) are all about *what kinds of types* a static checker can express and verify — inference is orthogonal to all of them, just a notation layer sitting on top.

A generic function's type signature, once written or inferred, still has to satisfy the rules the next Topic covers: how a language lets you write one function that works safely across many types without giving up static checking.
